Most existing models employ simple downsampling-ba...Show More Pooling and unpooling are indispensable in constructing hierarchical spherical convolutional neural networks (HS-CNNs). Most existing models employ simple downsampling-based pooling, which ignores the sampling theorem and cannot adapt to different spherical signals (with different spectra) and tasks (dependent on different frequency components), thus suffering a significant information loss. To address these, we propose a novel framework of HS-CNNs with lifting structures to learn adaptive spherical wavelets for pooling and unpooling, named LiftHS-CNNs. Specifically, we learn spherical wavelets with a lifting structure to adaptively partition the input signal into low- and high-frequency sub-bands, with the down-scaled representations for pooling generated to preserve more information in the low-frequency sub-band. We then propose an unpooling operation invertible to the lifting-based pooling for restoring the up-scaled representations, which can well preserve spectral characteristics of the original signal. **Published in:**IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence ( Early Access ) **Date of Publication:** 27 August 2025 **DOI:**10.1109/TPAMI.2025.3603601 Implementation of wavelet transform extrasystole heart sound with convolution method for feature extraction 2017 25th Signal Processing and Communications Applications Conference (SIU) Feature Extraction Using Wavelet Transform for Radar Emitter Signals 2009 WRI International Conference on Communications and Mobile Computing * US & Canada: +1 800 678 4333 * Worldwide: +1 732 981 0060 A public charity, IEEE is the world's largest technical professional organization dedicated to advancing technology for the benefit of humanity. * **US & Canada:** +1 800 678 4333 * **Worldwide:** +1 732 981 0060 * Privacy & Opting Out of Cookies A not-for-profit organization, IEEE is the world's largest technical professional organization dedicated to advancing technology for the benefit of humanity.

results.title: Hierarchical Merging | COSMOS
results.content: Hierarchical merging (or hierarchical clustering) is the process by which larger structures are formed through the continuous merging of smaller structures. The structures we see in the Universe today (galaxies, clusters, filaments, sheets and voids) are predicted to have formed in this way according to Cold Dark Matter cosmology (the current concordance model). For example, the formation of galaxies is thought to begin when small structures (perhaps no more massive than globular clusters) merge to form larger objects. These larger objects then merge to from even larger objects, which continue to merge until we arrive at the massive galaxies we see today in the local Universe. Small regions from the Hubble Ultra-Deep Field are full of examples of disturbed, interacting and merging galaxies. Nevertheless, hierarchical clustering models of galaxy formation make one very important prediction:. While young populations of stars have been observed in the centres of many galaxies, it is not yet clear whether these are a light ‘frosting’, perhaps the result of a secular evolution process, or whether they constitute evidence for major merger events. Astronomers are still investigating the relative importance of hierarchical clustering, primordial collapse and secular evolution in the formation of galaxies. Although we have talked about hierarchical clustering almost exclusively in the context of the formation of galaxies, it is also an important mechanism on much larger scales – those of galaxy clusters and superclusters. Galaxy Groups form through the merger of individual galaxies. An example of the ongoing process of hierarchical merging can be initiated with the Milky Way. Right now the Milky Way is undergoing minor mergers with a couple of dwarf galaxies in the Local Group, and also appears to be interacting with both the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. However, the ultimate fate of our Galaxy is to merge with Andromeda (the other large galaxy in the Local Group) to form a single, massive elliptical galaxy. This example, which traces the formation of a supercluster from a galactic scale, illustrates why hierarchical clustering is considered to be one of the most important processes in the formation of structure in the Universe.

results.title: Penrose Tiling Meets Multi-Scale GNNs: A Technical Walkthrough of Hierarchical Pooling & Synthetic Labelling | by Robert McMenemy | Medium
results.content: # Penrose Tiling Meets Multi-Scale GNNs: A Technical Walkthrough of Hierarchical Pooling & Synthetic Labelling. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have rapidly grown in popularity as a powerful method to model a variety of complex systems: social networks, molecular structures, recommendation systems, and more. Typically, GNNs assume that the underlying data is graph-based, with edges connecting certain pairs of nodes that have relevant relationships. However, in many real or synthetic scenarios, the geometry and topology of the graph can be **custom designed** to reflect properties that might help the network learn. **One such custom geometry** is based on *Penrose tilings*, an aperiodic tiling first popularized by the mathematician and physicist Sir Roger Penrose. Penrose tilings are multi-scale and never exactly repeat, yet they maintain local patterns that suggest both **hierarchical** and **self-similar** structure. This can be incredibly useful for GNNs, which often thrive on relational, multi-level data. In this blog article, we dive deep into the following:. 1. How to **generate** a Penrose-like tiling or deflation-based multi-scale Penrose tiling in Python. 2. How to **convert** that tiling into a graph structure (nodes + edges). 3.
